metadata.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
metadata.emergency_level: Chronic - acute exacerbations and respiratory failure are emergencies
metadata.severity: Progressive; graded by airflow limitation, symptoms and exacerbation risk

overview.short_description: A common, preventable and treatable chronic lung disease with persistent respiratory symptoms and PERSISTENT (largely irreversible) airflow limitation due to airway/alveolar abnormalities, usually from significant exposure to noxious particles or gases (mainly tobacco smoke).
overview.detailed_description: COPD is characterised by progressive, persistent airflow limitation confirmed by post-bronchodilator spirometry (FEV1/FVC <0.7). It typically presents after age 35 in smokers with chronic breathlessness, cough and sputum. Management centres on smoking cessation, inhaled therapy, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination, and prompt treatment of exacerbations. Distinguishing COPD from asthma (variable, reversible) is important, though they can coexist.
overview.pathophysiology: Chronic inflammation from inhaled irritants causes small-airway disease (obstructive bronchiolitis) and parenchymal destruction (emphysema), reducing elastic recoil and airflow, causing air trapping/hyperinflation and impaired gas exchange.
overview.etiology: Predominantly tobacco smoking; also biomass fuel smoke, occupational dusts/fumes, air pollution; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in a minority (younger, non-smokers, family history).
overview.incubation_period: Not applicable (develops over years of exposure).
overview.natural_history: Progressive decline in lung function and exercise tolerance; punctuated by exacerbations that accelerate decline and increase mortality; smoking cessation slows progression.
overview.prognosis: Variable; worse with severe airflow limitation, frequent exacerbations, low BMI, comorbidity, and continued smoking. Smoking cessation and appropriate therapy improve outcomes.

prevalence.value: A leading global cause of chronic morbidity; affects hundreds of millions and is a top cause of death worldwide (WHO/GOLD).

incidence.value: Increases with age and cumulative smoking exposure.

mortality.value: Among the leading causes of death globally (WHO).

epidemiology.sex_predominance: Historically male-predominant; rising in women with smoking patterns.
epidemiology.geographic_distribution: Worldwide; high burden where smoking and biomass exposure are common.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Tobacco smoking (main), biomass/solid-fuel smoke exposure, physical inactivity.
risk_factors.smoking: The dominant cause; cumulative exposure (pack-years) determines risk.
risk_factors.obesity: Not causal; low BMI worsens prognosis; obesity affects breathlessness.
risk_factors.hypertension: Common comorbidity (cardiovascular disease frequent in COPD).
risk_factors.pregnancy: Not typically relevant (COPD is a later-life disease).
risk_factors.travel: Air travel/altitude may cause hypoxia in advanced disease.
risk_factors.genetic_factors: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (consider if young/non-smoker/family history).
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Childhood respiratory infections, poorly-controlled asthma, recurrent chest infections.

symptoms.importance: Cardinal; typically persistent and progressive (vs variable in asthma)

symptoms.symptom: Fatigue, weight loss, reduced exercise tolerance (advanced)
Confusion/drowsiness, marked distress, cyanosis (severe exacerbation/CO2 retention)

negative_findings.finding: Marked symptom variability, reversibility, night-time waking, and strong atopy without smoking history

history_questions.question: Do you have a significant smoking (or biomass/occupational) exposure history?
Is the breathlessness persistent and progressive rather than variable/reversible?
How many exacerbations/courses of steroids or antibiotics and admissions in the last year?
Young, non-smoker, or family history of early emphysema?
Any weight loss, haemoptysis, or ankle swelling?

physical_examination.expected_finding: Prolonged expiration, wheeze, hyperinflation (barrel chest), reduced breath sounds; may be normal in mild disease
May be reduced/raised; important in exacerbations

physical_examination.examination: Signs of cor pulmonale (raised JVP, oedema)

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: May be chronically reduced; target 88-92% in those at risk of CO2 retention
vital_signs.bmi: Low BMI is a poor prognostic sign

laboratory_tests.test_name: FBC (polycythaemia/anaemia, eosinophils), alpha-1 antitrypsin (selective), BNP/ECG for comorbidity

laboratory_tests.indication: Severe exacerbation or chronic hypoxia assessment

imaging.when_needed: At diagnosis (exclude other pathology) and in exacerbations
imaging.expected_findings: Hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, bullae; excludes cancer/pneumonia/pneumothorax

imaging.when_needed: Diagnostic uncertainty, suspected bronchiectasis/malignancy, or surgical/bullae assessment

ecg.findings: Right heart strain, arrhythmia, or ischaemia in comorbidity.

other_diagnostic_tests.spirometry: Post-bronchodilator spirometry is REQUIRED to confirm persistent airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC <0.7).
other_diagnostic_tests.culture: Sputum culture in exacerbations not responding or with purulence

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Consider COPD in a patient >35 with a risk factor (usually smoking) and typical symptoms (exertional breathlessness, chronic cough/sputum, frequent winter infections). CONFIRM with post-bronchodilator spirometry showing FEV1/FVC <0.7 (persistent airflow obstruction). Assess symptoms (mMRC/CAT) and exacerbation risk (GOLD ABE grouping).

diagnostic_scores.value: GOLD grading of airflow limitation by FEV1 % predicted; symptom scores mMRC/CAT; GOLD groups A/B/E by symptoms and exacerbation history.

cutoff_values.value: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 defines airflow obstruction (GOLD). Target SpO2 88-92% in patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.

differential_diagnosis.differences: Variable/reversible airflow limitation, atopy, night symptoms, younger/non-smoker
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Are symptoms variable/reversible or steadily progressive?
Do you get breathless lying flat with ankle swelling?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Haemoptysis, weight loss, focal signs, mass on imaging
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any coughing up blood or weight loss?
Do you cough up large amounts of sputum most days?
Is your spirometry restrictive with fine crackles?

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a significant smoking history with persistent, progressive breathlessness (rather than variable/reversible)?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Smoking + persistent progressive symptoms -> COPD (confirm with spirometry)

diagnostic_questions.question: In an exacerbation: are you more breathless, is sputum increased/purulent, and are you confused/drowsy with low oxygen?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Confusion/drowsiness, marked hypoxia -> emergency (possible CO2 retention)

next_best_question.question: Are symptoms persistent/progressive, how many exacerbations last year, and any red flags (haemoptysis/weight loss)?
next_best_question.expected_answers: Typical COPD pattern / risk / red flags
next_best_question.branching_logic: Typical -> spirometry to confirm, start inhaled therapy + smoking cessation + rehab; frequent exacerbations -> escalate/prevent; red flags -> urgent CXR/cancer pathway

next_best_test.why: Required to confirm persistent airflow obstruction

next_best_test.test: Chest X-ray + FBC (+ alpha-1 antitrypsin if young/non-smoker)

red_flags.finding: Acute severe breathlessness with confusion/drowsiness, cyanosis, or exhaustion
red_flags.immediate_action: Emergency - controlled oxygen (target 88-92%), bronchodilators, steroids +/- antibiotics; assess for NIV/ventilation and CO2 retention

red_flags.finding: SpO2 falling, rising CO2/acidosis on blood gas
red_flags.immediate_action: Emergency - consider non-invasive ventilation; senior/critical-care input

red_flags.finding: Haemoptysis, weight loss, or new focal chest signs
Signs of cor pulmonale or new significant hypoxia
red_flags.immediate_action: Assess for long-term oxygen therapy and heart failure

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Severe exacerbation/respiratory failure (emergency); suspected lung cancer (urgent pathway); diagnostic uncertainty.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Severe/rapidly progressive disease, frequent exacerbations despite optimisation, suspected alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, assessment for oxygen/rehabilitation/surgery.

late: Cachexia and reduced quality of life
Increased cardiovascular disease and lung cancer risk

initial_management.supportive_care: SMOKING CESSATION is the single most important intervention; pulmonary rehabilitation; vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19); self-management plan; treat comorbidities; nutritional support.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): LAMA and/or LABA; ICS-containing combination; Short systemic corticosteroid course; Antibiotic. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_NG115.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Stop smoking, stay active, pulmonary rehabilitation, healthy weight, vaccinations, action plan for exacerbations.
initial_management.follow_up: Regular review of symptoms (mMRC/CAT), exacerbations, inhaler technique/adherence, spirometry, oxygenation, and comorbidities.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Inhaled bronchodilators (LABA and/or LAMA) as maintenance; add inhaled corticosteroid especially with asthmatic features/eosinophilia or frequent exacerbations (LABA/LAMA/ICS triple therapy for higher-risk); ensure correct inhaler technique. Exacerbations: increase bronchodilators, oral corticosteroids, antibiotics if infective (increased purulent sputum), controlled oxygen (target 88-92%), and NIV for hypercapnic respiratory failure.

patient_education.home_advice: COPD is long-term lung damage, usually from smoking. Stopping smoking is by far the most important step - it slows the disease. Use your inhalers correctly every day, stay active and do pulmonary rehab, and have your flu and pneumonia jabs. Learn to spot a flare-up (more breathless, more or discoloured phlegm) and have a plan. Get emergency help if you are severely breathless, drowsy or confused, or your lips look blue.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: الداء الرئوي الانسدادي المزمن تلف مزمن في الرئة، غالباً بسبب التدخين. التوقّف عن التدخين هو الأهم بلا منازع فهو يُبطئ المرض. استخدم بخّاخاتك بطريقة صحيحة يومياً، وحافظ على النشاط وأعِد التأهيل الرئوي، وخذ لقاحات الإنفلونزا والالتهاب الرئوي. تعلّم علامات النوبة (زيادة ضيق النفس أو زيادة/تغيّر لون البلغم) واحمل خطة. اطلب المساعدة الطارئة عند ضيق نفس شديد أو خمول أو تشوّش أو ازرقاق الشفتين.
patient_education.prevention: Never smoking / smoking cessation; reduce occupational and biomass exposure; vaccination.
patient_education.warning_signs: Increasing breathlessness, more or discoloured/purulent sputum, fever, drowsiness/confusion, or blue lips - seek urgent care.

prevention.vaccination: Influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID-19 vaccinations recommended.
prevention.lifestyle: Smoking cessation and avoidance of smoke/occupational exposures are primary prevention.
prevention.screening: No general screening; case-finding via spirometry in symptomatic smokers.

evidence.evidence_level: High - smoking cessation, inhaled therapy, pulmonary rehabilitation, and vaccination are evidence-based.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by NICE_NG115; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
